title: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: agents as 'newspapers on the internet', training associates, and the bet on specialised firm systems
author: Gabe Pereyra

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Pereyra accepts that agentic AI will reshape legal work and materially extends the cluster through a provider-side model in which firms build specialised, private AI systems for clients. He also frames adoption as a long-term redesign of client service, while leaving pricing, IP and the balance between AI delivery and direct legal work unresolved. He does not substantively address the cluster’s verification, error-propagation or governance concerns.
qs: And so what you need to do is build the infrastructure for the law firms to build these systems so they can work with their clients.
And to me, that's going to be the next question for the next, you know, decade or two is now I give you all of these agents or all of this AI, what is the new way that you work with clients?

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s infrastructure thesis and materially develops it by identifying secure, context-rich firm–client collaboration as Harvey’s strategic layer. He also sharpens the competitive uncertainty: foundation models may enable in-house substitution, while Harvey is betting on shared tooling that preserves and reorganises firm–client delivery.
qs: And then the other is that instead what you need is the tooling that I described to connect law firms  with their clients.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Pereyra accepts that effective legal AI depends on more than model capability and materially develops the proposition by identifying secure firm–client context infrastructure and firm-specific knowledge as inputs for both AI performance and associate learning. He also reinforces the cluster’s rejection of a simple split between strategic human work and routine automation, although his claims are largely experiential and predictive rather than measured.
qs: So I think right now a lot of it is engineering and product where the infrastructure we need to build is how do you help law firms structure all of their data and their collaboration with their clients so that you can get all of this context in one place so that AI is  super effective on those client matters.
And so if you think of the data that law firms have, one, it's very useful for them to train their own AI systems, but it's also super useful for them to train their associates.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Pereyra materially extends the cluster’s proposed reconstruction of apprenticeship by outlining firm-specific AI training systems that capture partner feedback and deliver role-specific curricula. He treats AI as a potential educational resource, but does not directly establish the cluster’s competence paradox or the need to preserve independent practice and supervised live work.
qs: And so if you think of the data that law firms have, one, it's very useful for them to train their own AI systems, but it's also super useful for them to train their associates.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI should reshape legal delivery and client relationships rather than merely automate individual tasks. He materially develops it through a concrete model of specialised, secure firm–client infrastructure that organises contextual data and enables new service models, while treating profitability and scaling outcomes as conditional rather than demonstrated. He does not substantially address the cluster’s apprenticeship or verification concerns.
qs: And so I think a lot of the the shift and where we think we'll differentiate is not just on the model layer, but really what is all of the infrastructure  that an AI first law firm is going to need to be as effective as possible.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s core view that Harvey aims to become workflow infrastructure rather than merely a legal assistant, and materially develops it through concrete ambitions for matter orchestration, structured firm data, secure firm–client collaboration and domain-specific modules. He also reinforces the cluster’s caution: these are strategic bets and engineering priorities, not demonstrated gains in accuracy, productivity or intensive adoption.
qs: And so I think a lot of the the shift and where we think we'll differentiate is not just on the model layer, but really what is all of the infrastructure  that an AI first law firm is going to need to be as effective as possible.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s core thesis that durable specialist value lies beyond the foundation model in contextual, domain-specific workflow layers. He materially extends it by framing Harvey as firm–client collaboration and matter-orchestration infrastructure, including structured data, security, ethical walls and specialised drafting modules, while treating broader service and pricing changes as predictions rather than established outcomes.
qs: And so I think a lot of the the shift and where we think we'll differentiate is not just on the model layer, but really what is all of the infrastructure  that an AI first law firm is going to need to be as effective as possible.

So I think right now a lot of it is engineering and product where the infrastructure we need to build is how do you help law firms structure all of their data and their collaboration with their clients so that you can get all of this context in one place so that AI is  super effective on those client matters.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: The source accepts that value depends on how Harvey is embedded in legal work, not access or usage volume alone. It materially extends the cluster by describing a supervised workflow in which senior lawyers review AI first passes before assigning structured corrective work to juniors, while also proposing morale and retention as early forms of return that may not appear in conventional financial measures. Its claims about emerging business returns remain anecdotal and unquantified.
qs: And I think what's so powerful about these models is as a partner, a senior associate, you can have the model take a first pass, look at that, and then give it to a junior associate and say, "Hey, these sections are correct.

I've argued to many firms that the single most important ROI of an AI personal assistant, whether it's Harvey, whether it's another one, um, is not going to show up yet on a P&L the way you're used to old ROI showing up.

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s central organisational-redesign proposition and materially develops it: firms could encode legal expertise into models, loosen the link between revenue and headcount, and reconsider client delivery, pricing, training and firm structure. He also preserves the synthesis’s uncertainty by making technology-like scale conditional on model quality and viable business models rather than claiming demonstrated transformation.
qs: And to me, that's going to be the next question for the next, you know, decade or two is now I give you all of these agents or all of this AI, what is the new way that you work with clients?

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s non-binary, hybrid view of AI across strategic and lower-level work, and materially extends it by framing service delivery, client collaboration, intellectual property and pricing as long-term firm-design questions. He does not, however, directly address verification, responsibility or the evidence on uneven productivity gains.
qs: It's really going to be a hybrid of both.
And to me, that's going to be the next question for the next, you know, decade or two is now I give you all of these agents or all of this AI, what is the new way that you work with clients?

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Pereyra accepts that AI will redesign legal-service production and economics rather than eliminate large firms or lawyers. He materially extends the cluster by specifying a firm-wide model built around specialised, private AI systems, client collaboration, data infrastructure, security and ethical walls, while predicting that firms may decouple revenue growth from headcount. These claims remain strategic forecasts rather than measured outcomes.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s framing of AI as service and organisational redesign rather than routine automation alone. He materially develops it by identifying concrete redesign questions around client relationships, delivery methods, jointly created intellectual property, pricing and collaboration, while treating outcomes for incumbent and AI-first firms as predictions rather than established effects.
qs: And to me, that's going to be the next question for the next, you know, decade or two is now I give you all of these agents or all of this AI, what is the new way that you work with clients?

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Pereyra accepts the core hybrid account: AI can automate lower-level work while also complementing lawyers in strategic work. He materially extends the proposition by arguing that this combination will require long-term redesign of client relationships, service delivery, intellectual property and pricing, although he offers forecasts rather than measured staffing or productivity evidence.
qs: It's really going to be a hybrid of both.
And to me, that's going to be the next question for the next, you know, decade or two is now I give you all of these agents or all of this AI, what is the new way that you work with clients?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s core claim that value comes from redesigning work and operating models rather than deploying isolated assistants. He materially extends it by advocating firm-wide AI infrastructure, practice-specific playbooks and context-specific ROI measurement, while predicting that encoded expertise could enable new forms of scale. His claims about technology-like margins and deal wins remain conditional or anecdotal, and he gives limited attention to verification and the jagged capability frontier.
qs: And so I think a lot of the the shift and where we think we'll differentiate is not just on the model layer, but really what is all of the infrastructure  that an AI first law firm is going to need to be as effective as possible.
And I think a lot of the challenge is it's different for every practice area and it depends on the client and how you structure it.

st.t: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
st.an: Pereyra accepts that effective legal AI depends on workflow infrastructure rather than model capability alone, and materially develops the proposition by specifying secure firm–client collaboration, ethical walls, structured data and shared matter context as prerequisites for useful AI. His claims are strategic product priorities and forecasts, not evidence that these mechanisms have resolved verification costs or trust.
qs: So I think right now a lot of it is engineering and product where the infrastructure we need to build is how do you help law firms structure all of their data and their collaboration with their clients so that you can get all of this context in one place so that AI is  super effective on those client matters.

st.t: Expert workflows: Legal context becomes product infrastructure
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s core view that AI’s significance lies in redesigning legal-service delivery rather than merely automating discrete junior tasks. He also supports converting firm-specific expertise into training infrastructure and anticipates hybrid use across routine and strategic work, while treating delivery, IP and pricing changes as open, long-term questions rather than proven transformation.
qs: And to me, that's going to be the next question for the next, you know, decade or two is now I give you all of these agents or all of this AI, what is the new way that you work with clients?

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Pereyra supports the cluster’s core framing of AI as an organisational and expertise-development challenge rather than simple lawyer substitution. He explicitly raises training as part of firm redesign and expects AI to combine strategic assistance with lower-level automation, though he does not provide evidence that succession routes are already weakening or propose the cluster’s specific funding and training remedies.
qs: I think the reality is with this technology is it's not going to be a binary split of like it's good at strategic, it's good at automating the lower level work.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Pereyra supports the cluster’s qualified, non-universal view: he treats AI-enabled insourcing as a possible strategy rather than an established wholesale shift, while betting that in-house teams will continue to need tools connecting them with outside firms. His emphasis on firm–client collaboration and the enduring value of complex, full-service advice reinforces selective substitution rather than general outside-counsel decline.
qs: One is there's one world where the foundation models get so good that in-house teams just bring in all of the outside council work, right?
And then the other is that instead what you need is the tooling that I described to connect law firms  with their clients.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: Pereyra supports the cluster’s core framing of AI as an operating-model transformation rather than merely a productivity tool. He anticipates changes to client relationships, service delivery, firm organisation, training, intellectual property and pricing, while presenting these as unresolved areas for experimentation rather than supplying a distinct model or evidence of market-wide change.
qs: And to me, that's going to be the next question for the next, you know, decade or two is now I give you all of these agents or all of this AI, what is the new way that you work with clients?

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s central proposition that AI value requires redesigning legal production rather than merely adopting tools. He specifically links institutional absorption to client service delivery, firm-wide workflows, pricing, embedded expertise and potentially new scaling economics, while presenting the larger-firm and technology-margin outcomes as conditional predictions rather than established effects.
qs: And to me, that's going to be the next question for the next, you know, decade or two is now I give you all of these agents or all of this AI, what is the new way that you work with clients?

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: Pereyra accepts the cluster’s central proposition that AI-driven legal transformation is an organisational and commercial redesign challenge, not merely task automation. He specifically identifies client relationships, service delivery, jointly built intellectual property and pricing as unresolved firm-design questions, while treating strategic assistance and lower-level automation as complementary.
qs: And to me, that's going to be the next question for the next, you know, decade or two is now I give you all of these agents or all of this AI, what is the new way that you work with clients?
What is the IP as you build these systems with your clients?

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: Pereyra supports the application-layer thesis by presenting secure, context-rich client–law-firm infrastructure as Harvey’s strategic source of value. He also frames foundation-model insourcing as a competing possible strategy, reinforcing that Harvey’s defensibility is a bet rather than an outcome proved by commercial traction.
qs: But then I think what becomes the really interesting AI research challenge and what our bet is is I think there's kind of going to be two competing strategies of how you can service in-house teams.

kp.k: Agent workforces may be transitional product designs
kp.d: Pereyra treats human analogies as useful for interaction design but predicts that mature AI systems will not simply reproduce human workforces. His newspaper-to-news-feed analogy suggests that products will eventually be redesigned around the technology's distinctive capabilities rather than existing organisational forms; this is a forecast, not an observed legal-market outcome.
qs: My intuition is what these a lot of these systems end up looking like though will not be oh we just copy what humans do and just scale up agents that way.
just trying to build agents and then build agent workforces is kind of the equivalent of let's take newspapers and and put them on the internet.

kp.k: Conversational assistants may evolve into structured matter workflows
kp.d: Pereyra describes parallel product directions: a colleague-like interface through which partners delegate tasks and retrieve firm or client information, and longer-term domain-specific workflow modules. Fund formation illustrates his projected transition from an assistant helping with work to structured modules drafting partnership agreements and side letters.
qs: we always had the term partner interface
They email some task to their associate, the associate goes and uses all this legal tech and then gives them a nicely formatted answer.
And right now, you can use Harvey and it's an assistant to do this.
here's a module that drafts the LPA. Here's a module that drafts the side letter.

kp.k: Firm knowledge could support contextual associate education
kp.d: Pereyra reports current educational use and conversations with firms, while identifying a larger prospective opportunity: capturing client-specific practice knowledge and partner feedback so associates can ask why work is structured a particular way. Unlike programming knowledge widely available online, much of this legal context remains inside firms. He envisages infrastructure and curricula tailored to practice areas and seniority.
qs: you can't ask for this client in this type of transaction, why am I structuring it this way? How does our firm usually do this?
if you think of the data that law firms have, one, it's very useful for them to train their own AI systems, but it's also super useful for them to train their associates.
I think people are using it now and then there's a bunch of infrastructure you can build around it to build curriculums

kp.k: AI offers a less intimidating channel for questions
kp.d: Both speakers connect AI-supported learning with reluctance to ask colleagues basic questions. Abramowitz recounts being criticised during his first-year review for asking too quickly rather than searching himself. Pereyra sees a substantial educational opportunity in allowing users to ask questions they would hesitate to put to managers, teams or investors; these are experiential observations rather than measured training outcomes.
qs: a lot of times you don't want to ask your manager some of these questions
one of the partners mentioned that you were too quick to like come back and like ask a question.
And so I think that to me is going to be a massive educational opportunity.

kp.k: Senior lawyers use AI to improve delegation
kp.d: Pereyra qualifies Abramowitz's suggestion that partners obtain the greatest utility: younger people more commonly use the technology, but some partners at leading firms reportedly use it 3 to 5 hours a day. He describes a human-in-the-loop delegation pattern in which a senior lawyer checks an AI first pass, identifies correct and missing sections, and gives a junior a more explicit assignment. No usage sample or systematic comparison is supplied.
qs: I think younger people use this more but we have partners at kind of the top firms in the world that are using this you know 3 to 5 hours a day
you can have the model take a first pass, look at that, and then give it to a junior associate and say, "Hey, these sections are correct. It missed this. Can you go fix this?"
Not just how do I get answers, but how do I communicate better to the folks that I'm working with?

kp.k: GPT-4 reportedly changed Harvey's target market
kp.d: Pereyra retrospectively identifies early access to GPT-4 as the inflection point that made corporate legal work appear feasible. He says earlier models led the founders to consider consumer applications, whereas his cofounder's 14-hour exploration of the newer model suggested substantial overlap with associate work. This is a founder's account of product discovery, not a benchmark of legal capability.
qs: we were looking at consumer because it just couldn't do big law like corporate legal work.
Winston just went in his room for 14 hours and just played with it and came out and was just like this can do so much of like what I did as an associate.

kp.k: Differentiation shifts from models to law-firm infrastructure
kp.d: Pereyra regards foundation-model providers as indirect competitors likely to continue professional-service verticalisation. Harvey's stated strategy is not merely to produce the best legal assistant, but to improve firms' businesses through team workflows, matter orchestration, new service delivery and client collaboration. These are strategic intentions rather than demonstrated profitability findings.
qs: I think all of these companies will do some professional service or verticalization but I think their focus is in improving the models
the goal isn't to make the best legal model or the best legal assistant.
It is really how do you help these law firms become more profitable or improve their business.
How do you help the law firm orchestrate all of the client matters they're working on?

kp.k: Specialised systems compete with potential in-house substitution
kp.d: Pereyra sets out two possible futures for corporate legal departments: general-purpose models become capable enough to bring outside-counsel work in-house, or firms remain involved through specialised AI and direct work connected to clients. Harvey bets on the latter, conditional on firm expertise being sufficiently specialised and private that general-purpose foundation models do not capture it. He presents this explicitly as a strategic bet and long-term research problem.
qs: there's one world where the foundation models get so good that in-house teams just bring in all of the outside council work
So the law firms can build AI or do the work directly to help their clients.
the bet there is how much of what these law firms are doing is so specialized and so private that it doesn't go in the foundation models
our bet is to build these very specialized AI systems.

kp.k: Client collaboration requires security and contextual data infrastructure
kp.d: Pereyra says much of Harvey's present challenge is engineering and product work that structures firm data and client collaboration before more ambitious AI research becomes possible. He identifies security, ethical walls and data problems as requirements for joint enterprise–law-firm systems, potentially including AI trained on the relationship. These are infrastructure priorities, not claims that specific professional-rule obligations have been resolved.
qs: how do you allow enterprises and their law firms to collaborate together and solving all of the security the ethical walls those data problems

how do you help law firms structure all of their data and their collaboration with their clients so that you can get all of this context in one place so that AI is super effective on those client matters.

kp.k: Incumbent and new firms may need similar platforms
kp.d: Abramowitz proposes that AI-first breakaway firms could undermine Harvey's incumbent customer base. Pereyra responds that the platform should serve both established and new firms, whose infrastructure needs he expects to resemble each other. He also argues that full-service capability and complex work remain reasons for large firms to persist, while allowing that smaller breakaways may emerge in some areas.
qs: our hope is that the platform we build would serve both of these customers.
I think probably the infrastructure both of those firms end up needing actually looks rather similar.
really the value is being full service being able to handle this very complex work that it's not clear to me like one or two partners can go off and and replicate what these big law firms do.

kp.k: AI affects strategic work as well as routine tasks
kp.d: Rejecting a clean division between mundane automation and human strategy, Pereyra reports users applying AI to high-level strategy, including preparation for Supreme Court arguments. He predicts a hybrid of strategic and lower-level applications. The reported examples carry no task-level evaluation or outcome evidence.
qs: I think there's even some folks that are using this to prep for like Supreme Court arguments and things like that.
it's not going to be a binary split of like it's good at strategic, it's good at automating the lower level work.
It's really going to be a hybrid of both.

kp.k: Lawyers face service-design and business-model questions
kp.d: Over the next decade or two, Pereyra expects firms to confront organisational questions analogous to those raised by the internet and personal computers: how to organise work, train people and deliver services. He highlights client relationships, intellectual property in jointly built systems and new pricing models, recommending practical use of AI as a prerequisite for thinking through these changes rather than prescribing a particular fee arrangement.
qs: that's going to be the next question for the next, you know, decade or two is now I give you all of these agents or all of this AI, what is the new way that you work with clients?
How do you deliver the services? What is the IP as you build these systems with your clients? What are the new pricing models?
you really need to use this technology to start thinking about it

kp.k: Encoded expertise could loosen revenue's dependence on headcount
kp.d: Pereyra predicts much larger law firms if models become sufficiently capable and firms successfully encode expertise and develop suitable business models. His proposed mechanism is movement from service-like scaling and margins toward technology-like economics, rather than merely adding lawyers. Abramowitz separately suggests polarisation into very large or very small firms; no staffing ratios or realised margin changes are reported.
qs: I think you'll have much larger law firms
your revenue is just linearly tied to your headcount
if these models get good enough and you're able to figure out how to take your legal expertise and put it in a model and figure out the right business model
you can get kind of more tech scaling and tech margins than service scaling and service margins

kp.k: Commercial ROI claims remain practice-specific and partly aspirational
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that morale and retention are the principal early returns, drawing on anecdotal accounts of managing-partner purchasing. Pereyra acknowledges intangible value but stresses quantification, reports firms winning work by pitching AI-enabled collaboration, and describes ongoing practice-specific measurement. The suggested 30% improvement in profits per partner is explicitly an eventual ideal sales proposition, not an achieved result.
qs: But the primary ROI is the employee morale and lawyer retention.
as a business, you still do need to find ways of quantifying this.
we've seen law firms start winning deals by pitching in that way.
the ultimate pitch for Harvey would be we can improve your profits per partner by 30%. or something like that, right? Like that's the holy grail ROI story.
it's different for every practice area and it depends on the client and how you structure it.

kp.k: Access-to-justice ambitions coexist with commercial constraints
kp.d: Pereyra describes consumer law and access to justice as early interests and a continuing mission, while emphasising the need for revenue. He reports beginning more work with court systems largely outside the United States and expresses intentions to work with US courts and expand consumer applications. The transcript offers no evidence of improved public access or court outcomes.
qs: when we first started the company, we looked at things like could we do consumer law, access to justice.
you do need to build a business and you do need to get revenue
we're starting to do more with court systems largely outside of the US but eventually want to do this with the US

kp.k: Capital-intensive competition motivates rapid vendor expansion
kp.d: Asked why Harvey raises substantial venture capital rather than remaining lean, Pereyra frames financing as a means to execute a clear product strategy quickly. He cites rapid hiring, office openings, potential acquisitions and expensive AI talent and compute, arguing that the pace of foundation-model companies leaves limited room for bootstrapping. This is his strategic justification, not evidence that all legal-AI vendors require the same model.
qs: it really depends on company strategy, industry, and and those dynamics.
the goal is really to scale as quickly as possible.
we're hiring super quickly. We're opening offices. Um, we're thinking about acquisitions.
it's not clear to me you have the luxury to to bootstrap because it's moving so quickly.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Pereyra predicts that legal AI will evolve beyond human-like assistants and agent workforces toward domain-specific, structured workflows.
pts.d: Pereyra treats simply reproducing human workforces with agents as an early-stage design approach, analogous to putting newspapers online rather than developing news feeds. He envisages both a conversational 'partner interface' for delegating tasks and accessing firm/client information, and longer-term modules for particular parts of matters, such as drafting fund formation documents. These are product predictions, not reports of fully autonomous legal practice already operating.

pts.k: Pereyra identifies firm-specific AI tutoring as a major opportunity for associate development.
pts.d: He says AI is already used for learning and could teach associates both general legal concepts and the firm's particular approaches to clients and transactions. The proposed advance is to incorporate internal knowledge, partner feedback and senior-associate intuition, then build role-specific curricula. He distinguishes this private contextual knowledge from programming knowledge readily available on the internet. This is an augmentation and education claim, not a prediction that junior lawyers disappear.

pts.k: Pereyra reports substantive partner use and says AI improves delegation as well as answering questions.
pts.d: He qualifies the host's suggestion about partner adoption: younger people use AI more commonly, but some partners at leading firms use Harvey extensively. Partners and senior associates can obtain a first draft, identify what is correct or missing, and give juniors a more structured assignment. This workflow explicitly retains senior human review and junior follow-up; the reference to an '80% structure' is an illustrative description, not a measured accuracy rate.

pts.k: Pereyra says AI supports high-level legal strategy as well as lower-level automation.
pts.d: He reports use for Supreme Court argument preparation and rejects a simple division in which AI only automates mundane work while lawyers retain strategy. His claim is that both types of work will involve AI. Over the next decade or two, he expects lawyers' central challenge to include redesigning service delivery, client relationships, intellectual property arrangements and pricing around AI.

pts.k: Pereyra's strategic bet is that specialised, private legal knowledge will sustain firm-built AI systems rather than all outside-counsel work moving in-house.
pts.d: He outlines two competing scenarios: general-purpose foundation models become capable enough for corporate legal departments to internalise outside-counsel work, or law firms use specialised systems and shared infrastructure to serve those clients. He favours the latter because relevant expertise and information may be too specialised and private to enter general-purpose models. He presents insourcing as an alternative scenario, not his own unconditional forecast.

pts.k: Pereyra expects legal-AI competition to move beyond individual assistants toward infrastructure for firms, teams and client collaboration.
pts.d: He regards foundation-model providers as indirect competitors that will increasingly develop professional-services capabilities. Harvey's proposed differentiation is infrastructure that helps firms improve their businesses: organising matters, coordinating teams, collaborating with enterprise clients and delivering services differently. He expects much of this infrastructure to serve both established large firms and new AI-first firms. Harvey is described here as a software/platform supplier, not as an ALSP delivering legal work.

pts.k: Pereyra predicts continued demand for large full-service firms and the possibility of much larger firms with technology-like economics.
pts.d: He argues that one or two departing partners cannot clearly replicate the full-service capacity for complex work of major firms, while allowing that new small firms will emerge in some areas. His larger-firm forecast is conditional on sufficiently capable models, encoding legal expertise and finding appropriate business models. He predicts the possibility of revenue scaling less directly with headcount and achieving technology-like margins; he does not specify staffing shapes or employment-loss estimates.

pts.k: Pereyra reports that AI-enabled client pitches are helping firms win work, while presenting quantified profit improvement as a future goal.
pts.d: He says clients want their firms to use AI and that firms have won deals by proposing new AI-enabled ways of working together. Harvey is beginning practice-by-practice work on ROI measurement and service-delivery playbooks. The example of improving profits per partner by 30% is explicitly an aspirational sales proposition, not a demonstrated result.
